questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and post feedback. Feedback must be actionable, and false positives erode developer trust.
questions.stem: The CI review prompt already lists the four parts every comment must contain: file location, issue, severity and suggested fix. Developers complain that comments still vary a lot. Some leave out the severity, others write a paragraph with no concrete fix, and the order of the parts changes from run to run. The team wants more consistent comments with minimal changes to the pipeline. What should you do first?

options.text: Rewrite the format instructions in capital letters and add a closing line telling Claude that comments missing any part will be rejected.
Add two or three complete example comments to the prompt, each showing location, issue, severity and suggested fix in the exact layout you want.
Move the review job to a larger model on the assumption that a stronger model follows multi-part formatting instructions more reliably.
Add a final step asking Claude to reread each comment it wrote and confirm that all four parts are present before it posts.

questions.explanation: When detailed instructions alone still give inconsistent output, **few-shot examples** are the most effective next step. A few concrete examples show the exact layout, level of detail and tone you want, which written rules describe only loosely. Claude's prompting guide calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer output format and structure. This is also a small change: you edit only the prompt.

whyWrong.A: Louder wording and threats repeat the same instructions that already failed. The format is still described only in the abstract, so it stays inconsistent.
whyWrong.C: A bigger model costs more and does not fix the cause. The prompt never *shows* what a good comment looks like.
whyWrong.D: Self-checking adds tokens and latency, and the model checks against the same vague picture of the format it already has. Examples set that picture up front.

questions.mindset: When instructions are already clear but output still varies, show the format with examples instead of repeating the rules more loudly.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and post feedback. Feedback must be actionable, and false positives erode developer trust.
questions.stem: The automated PR reviewer keeps flagging code the team has deliberately accepted. Examples include a broad exception handler inside a retry wrapper that logs and re-raises, and SQL built from constants inside a migration script. Developers have started ignoring the bot. The prompt already says 'only report genuine problems' and lists the review categories. Which change is MOST likely to cut these false positives while still catching real issues in code patterns the team hasn't seen yet?

options.text: Add an instruction telling Claude to be conservative and to report only findings it is highly confident about, skipping anything borderline.
Have Claude give each finding a confidence score from 1 to 10 and post only findings scored 8 or higher to the pull request.
Keep a growing list in the prompt of every exact code snippet the team has accepted so far and tell Claude never to flag those snippets.
Add a few examples that pair an accepted pattern with a similar genuine defect, each explaining why one is fine and the other is a real issue.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that **contrast acceptable patterns with genuine issues**, and explain the reasoning, teach the boundary the model has been getting wrong. Because each example says *why*, Claude can apply the same judgment to new code it has not seen, so real defects still get caught. That is the 'enabling generalization' part of the question.

whyWrong.A: 'Be conservative' is a vague directive. It doesn't say where the line is, so it tends to suppress real findings as well as false ones, or it changes nothing.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. The model is already confident about these false positives, so a threshold would let them through.
whyWrong.C: An exact-match exclusion list only covers snippets already listed. It doesn't generalize to new variations and keeps growing the prompt.

questions.mindset: Teach the decision boundary with contrasting examples that explain the reasoning; avoid vague caution and self-rated confidence.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system uses Claude to pull structured data out of unstructured documents, validates the output against JSON schemas, and feeds downstream systems. It must stay accurate and handle edge cases gracefully.
questions.stem: Your extraction tool's schema has a `dimensions` field that is required but nullable. On spec sheets with a clean table, extraction is nearly perfect. On supplier documents that give sizes in running text, such as 'roughly two feet wide by 18 inches deep', or in a footnote under a photo, the model often returns null even though the information is there. Which change addresses this MOST directly?

options.text: Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from narrative text, footnotes and informal measurements, with the normalized value for each.
Make `dimensions` non-nullable in the schema so the model must always return a value instead of falling back to null when it is unsure.
Wrap the extraction call in a loop that retries the same prompt up to five times whenever `dimensions` comes back null.
Add a sentence to the prompt saying that dimensions may appear anywhere in the document and that Claude should search the whole document carefully.

questions.explanation: Null results for fields that *are* in the document, concentrated in one kind of document structure, point to a gap in the model's understanding of those formats. Few-shot examples that show correct extraction from **varied document structures and informal measurements** directly fix empty or null extraction of required fields, and they also show how to normalize the values.

whyWrong.B: Forcing a non-null value would make the model invent dimensions for documents that truly lack them. That removes a safety valve and adds hallucinated data.
whyWrong.C: Retrying an unchanged prompt mostly repeats the same miss. Retries help when you feed back specific errors, not when the model doesn't know the format.
whyWrong.D: A general reminder to 'search carefully' doesn't show what informal or embedded measurements look like or how to convert them.

questions.mindset: If extraction fails on particular document formats, show those formats with worked examples instead of adding pressure or retries.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. You are building a support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). The target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while still escalating the right cases.
questions.stem: The support agent mishandles borderline cases. It escalates a simple address change because the customer sounds angry, and it tries to resolve a disputed charge on its own when policy says that case needs a human. You plan to add few-shot examples to the system prompt. Which TWO properties will make these examples MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Lots of examples of routine, unambiguous requests, so the agent gets plenty of practice on the cases it sees most often.
Examples focused on the ambiguous boundary cases, where escalating and resolving both look reasonable at first glance.
Examples that all share the same wording, structure and customer tone, so the agent can pattern-match them easily.
Examples that only show successful autonomous resolutions, to push the agent toward the 80% first-contact resolution target.
Each example briefly says why the chosen action beat the plausible alternative, such as why anger alone doesn't justify escalation.

questions.explanation: Effective examples are **targeted at the ambiguous cases** where the agent goes wrong, and they **show the reasoning** for picking one action over a plausible alternative. A handful is enough: the exam guide talks about 2 to 4 targeted examples, and Claude's prompting docs suggest 3 to 5 in general. Explaining the reasoning lets the agent apply the same criteria to new situations, for example that customer sentiment doesn't measure case complexity.

whyWrong.A: Routine cases are already handled correctly. Adding them uses tokens and adds nothing at the boundary where errors happen.
whyWrong.C: Uniform examples teach surface patterns. Claude's guidance asks for diverse examples so the model doesn't pick up unintended patterns.
whyWrong.D: Showing only one outcome biases the agent against escalation, which makes it worse at the disputed-charge cases that must go to a human.

questions.mindset: Spend few-shot examples on the confusing boundary cases, and explain why each choice is right.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and post feedback. Feedback must be actionable, and false positives erode developer trust.
questions.stem: Your CI test-generation step uses three few-shot examples to show how to spot untested branches, such as an early return for empty input or a fallback path when a cache misses. Each example explains why that branch needs its own test. Coverage of untested branches has improved a lot, including for branch types the examples never mention. A teammate proposes replacing the three examples with a 60-row table in the prompt that maps specific code shapes to 'needs test' or 'skip', saying it will be more complete. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Adopt the table. An exhaustive mapping removes ambiguity and gives more predictable results than a small set of examples.
Adopt the table but keep a single example, so the prompt stays complete without growing large enough to slow down the review job.
Keep the reasoned examples. Add one or two new ones only when you find a category of missed branch, because the examples already generalize.
Remove the examples and the table, and instead instruct Claude to write a test for every branch it finds so that coverage is guaranteed.

questions.explanation: The evidence shows the examples work **and generalize**: coverage improved even for branch types they never mention. Reasoned few-shot examples teach a judgment the model can apply to new patterns. A lookup table only matches the cases it lists, uses many more tokens, and still misses whatever shape comes next. The right move is to keep what works and add a targeted example when a new category of miss appears.

whyWrong.A: A table only matches what it lists and doesn't teach the reasoning. It is the 'matching pre-specified cases' approach that few-shot examples are meant to improve on.
whyWrong.B: This still swaps a working, reasoned approach for a brittle lookup and adds tokens. The measured results give no reason for the change.
whyWrong.D: 'Test every branch' removes judgment altogether. It produces low-value tests for trivial branches and ignores what the team found about which branches matter.

questions.mindset: Examples that carry reasoning generalize to new cases; exhaustive rule tables do not. Don't replace something that measurably works.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A coordinator agent built with the Claude Agent SDK delegates to subagents that search the web, analyze documents, synthesize findings and write cited reports.
questions.stem: The document-analysis subagent pulls source citations out of papers so the report writer can cite them. It does well on papers with numbered bibliographies but often returns empty citation lists for papers that use author-year citations in the text, and it mixes up methodology details that sit inside the results section. Which change is the MOST proportionate fix?

options.text: Add a separate subagent for each citation style and a classifier that sends each paper to the matching subagent before extraction starts.
Add a few examples to the subagent's prompt showing correct extraction from author-year papers and from papers that bury methodology in results.
Write a regex preprocessor that converts all author-year citations into a numbered bibliography before the document reaches the subagent.
Raise the subagent's max_tokens and tell it to take more time so it can read long papers more thoroughly before returning citations.

questions.explanation: The failures follow **document structure** (inline author-year citations, methodology embedded in other sections). Few-shot examples that show correct handling of each structure are the documented, low-effort fix, and they leave the architecture as it is.

whyWrong.A: Separate subagents plus a router is an over-engineered first step. It adds coordination overhead before the cheap prompt fix has been tried.
whyWrong.C: Citation formats vary too much for regex to rewrite reliably, and this doesn't help with methodology details embedded in other sections.
whyWrong.D: The problem isn't length or output space. A bigger token budget doesn't teach the model to recognize author-year citations.

questions.mindset: Fix structure-specific extraction misses with targeted examples before adding agents or preprocessing.

questions.stem: An invoice-extraction prompt includes four few-shot examples. In every example the source invoice contains a purchase-order number and the output has a filled-in `po_number`. The schema marks `po_number` as nullable. In production, about 30% of invoices have no PO number, yet the model almost always returns a value, usually another reference number of similar shape taken from elsewhere on the page. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Add a sentence to the prompt saying that the purchase-order number must never be guessed and should come only from the invoice.
Change `po_number` from nullable to optional so that the model can leave the field out of its output entirely when it is unsure.
Add a validation step that rejects any `po_number` that doesn't match your PO format and retries the call with the error included.
Replace one example with an invoice that has no PO number and show `po_number: null`, so the examples cover the absent-field case.

questions.explanation: The examples taught an unintended pattern: *`po_number` is always filled in*. Examples are a strong signal, so the model copies them. Claude's guidance says examples should be **diverse and cover edge cases**. Adding an example where the field is missing and returns null directly removes the false pattern and cuts hallucinated values.

whyWrong.A: An abstract instruction competes with four concrete examples that all show a value, and the examples usually win. The cause is still there.
whyWrong.B: Changing nullable to optional doesn't change the behavior. The examples still teach the model to always produce a value.
whyWrong.C: Format validation is a good safety net, but the stem says the invented values have the same shape as real PO numbers, so most pass the check. It also pays for a retry that repeats the same skewed examples. It treats the symptom, not the cause.

questions.mindset: Few-shot examples teach whatever pattern they share, including mistakes. Make them diverse and include the 'field is absent' case.

questions.stem: An architecture review lists five open problems across your Claude-based systems. For which TWO is adding few-shot examples the most appropriate primary fix? Choose TWO.

options.text: The CI reviewer labels near-identical findings 'major' in one PR and 'minor' in the next, because the severity guidance is fuzzy.
The support agent must never call process_refund for amounts above $500, but it sometimes does when a customer is persistent.
About 1 in 200 extraction responses has malformed JSON that crashes the downstream parser, even though the prompt asks for valid JSON.
Customers write 'cancel it' to mean an order, a subscription or a scheduled delivery, and the agent picks the wrong meaning inconsistently.
The agent picks lookup_order when it should pick get_customer because both tool descriptions are a single vague line.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are best for **consistency and judgment in ambiguous cases**. Severity calibration (A) and resolving what an ambiguous request means (D) are both judgment calls that worked examples improve. The other three need a different kind of fix. A hard business limit needs a **deterministic control**. JSON syntax needs **structured outputs / strict tool use**. Tool confusion caused by thin descriptions needs **better tool descriptions** first.

whyWrong.B: A financial hard limit needs a guarantee: a hook or code-level check that blocks the call. Examples only make a violation less likely.
whyWrong.C: Syntax reliability is solved by schema-constrained output (structured outputs or strict tool use). Examples can't guarantee valid JSON.
whyWrong.E: Thin descriptions are the root cause. The documented first step is to expand the tool descriptions. Few-shot examples here add tokens without fixing them.

questions.mindset: Use examples for judgment and consistency; use schemas, hooks and code for guarantees; fix the tool descriptions when they cause wrong tool choices.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and post feedback. Feedback must be actionable, and false positives erode developer trust.
questions.stem: Finance asks the platform team to cut Claude API spend in the CI/CD system. Five workloads currently use synchronous calls. Which TWO are the best candidates to move to the Message Batches API? Choose TWO.

options.text: The security review that has to pass before a pull request can be merged.
The assistant that answers developer questions in the team's chat channel.
The nightly job that generates missing unit tests for the whole repository.
The check that summarizes a PR's risk while the author waits at the merge page.
The weekly audit that scores each service's dependency hygiene for a Monday report.

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API cuts cost by 50%, but processing can take **up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency**. That suits **non-blocking, latency-tolerant** work such as nightly test generation and weekly audits. Anything a person or a merge gate is waiting on should stay synchronous.

whyWrong.A: A pre-merge gate is blocking. A batch can take up to 24 hours, so merges could stall for a day.
whyWrong.B: Interactive chat needs answers within seconds, and batch has no latency guarantee.
whyWrong.D: The author is waiting for this check at merge time, which makes it latency-sensitive like any blocking check.

questions.mindset: Match the API to the latency need: batch for work nobody is waiting on, synchronous calls for anything that blocks a person or process.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system uses Claude to pull structured data out of unstructured documents, validates the output against JSON schemas, and feeds downstream systems. It must stay accurate and handle edge cases gracefully.
questions.stem: Insurance claim documents arrive continuously. The contract with the downstream team guarantees extracted data within 36 hours of a document's arrival. You will collect documents and submit them on a fixed schedule through the Message Batches API, and you plan for the full 24-hour processing window (ignore retrieval and post-processing time). What is the LEAST frequent submission schedule that still guarantees the 36-hour commitment?

options.text: Submit once every 24 hours, matching the batch processing window.
Submit once every 36 hours, matching the contractual commitment.
Submit once every 12 hours, leaving room for the full 24-hour window.
Submit once every 4 hours, the interval your other batch pipelines already use.

questions.explanation: Worst case, a document arrives just after a submission and waits a full interval, then takes up to 24 hours to process. To stay within 36 hours: interval + 24 ≤ 36, so the interval must be **12 hours or less**. Twelve hours is the least frequent schedule that still guarantees the deadline.

whyWrong.A: 24 + 24 = 48 hours in the worst case, which breaks the 36-hour commitment.
whyWrong.B: 36 + 24 = 60 hours in the worst case, far beyond the commitment.
whyWrong.D: Every 4 hours meets the deadline but isn't the *least* frequent schedule that does. It adds batches and overhead you don't need.

questions.mindset: For an SLA, plan for the worst case: maximum wait before submission plus the full batch window.

questions.stem: A Message Batches job extracts clauses from 10,000 contracts. When the batch ends, 9,770 results succeeded and 230 errored. Of the errors, 180 are invalid-request errors from contracts too long for the model's context window, and 50 are transient server errors. What is the MOST efficient way to finish the job?

options.text: Resubmit only the 230 failed requests found by custom_id: chunk the 180 oversized contracts and resend the other 50 unchanged.
Resubmit the full 10,000-request batch with a higher max_tokens value so that the long contracts have enough room to complete.
Resubmit all 230 failed requests exactly as before, since batch errors are usually temporary and tend to clear on a second attempt.
Move the remaining 230 contracts to synchronous calls with an instruction to summarize each contract before extracting the clauses.

questions.explanation: Use `custom_id` to find exactly which requests failed and resubmit **only those**, with a fix suited to each cause. Oversized documents need **chunking**, because resending them unchanged will fail again. Transient server errors can be retried as they are. Errored requests aren't billed, and the 9,770 successes don't need to be redone.

whyWrong.B: Reprocessing 9,770 successful requests wastes time and money. max_tokens limits *output* length, so it can't fix an input that is too large for the context window.
whyWrong.C: The 180 context-limit failures are deterministic. They will fail again unless the input changes.
whyWrong.D: A long input still won't fit in a synchronous call, and 'summarize first' risks losing the exact clause text the job needs to extract.

questions.mindset: After a batch, resubmit only the failed custom_ids, and change the request for anything that will fail the same way again.

questions.stem: A developer submits 5,000 product descriptions in a Message Batch, in the same order as rows in a spreadsheet. When the batch ends, the script writes result 1 to row 1, result 2 to row 2 and so on. QA finds many products with descriptions belonging to other products. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Sort the results by creation timestamp before writing them back so that they line up with the original submission order.
Split the work into batches of 100 requests so that the results are small enough to come back in the order they were submitted.
Switch to synchronous calls, since only the synchronous Messages API keeps a fixed relationship between requests and responses.
Give each request a custom_id set to the product's row key, and write each result back by looking up its custom_id.

questions.explanation: Batch results **can come back in any order**. Every request has a unique `custom_id` (1 to 64 characters: letters, digits, hyphens and underscores), and that field is the documented way to match each result to its request. Setting it to a business key such as the row or product ID makes the write-back reliable.

whyWrong.A: No ordering guarantee exists to rebuild. Sorting by time doesn't connect a result to the request it answers.
whyWrong.B: Smaller batches still don't guarantee order. They only make the mismatches rarer and harder to spot.
whyWrong.C: This gives up the 50% saving because of a misunderstanding. Batch results can be matched reliably with custom_id.

questions.mindset: Never rely on position in batch results; match each result by custom_id.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system uses Claude to pull structured data out of unstructured documents, validates the output against JSON schemas, and feeds downstream systems. It must stay accurate and handle edge cases gracefully.
questions.stem: Your extraction agent runs synchronously and costs too much. For each document it calls a `lookup_vendor` tool you implemented, which takes the supplier tax ID printed in a fixed header block (your ingestion code already parses that ID with a regex) and returns the vendor's canonical record from your database. Claude then extracts the line items and finishes the record using that canonical data. The volume is 400,000 documents a month, and next-day turnaround is acceptable. You want to move to the Message Batches API. What is the BEST design?

options.text: Submit the documents as a batch with `lookup_vendor` defined in each request. The batch runs the tool call and passes the result back to Claude inside that request.
Keep the whole pipeline synchronous, because the Message Batches API can't accept requests that include tool definitions.
Run the vendor lookup in your own code before submission and put the canonical record in each request, so every document completes in a single turn.
Run a batch that stops at each tool call, then submit the tool results as a second batch, then a third batch for any follow-up calls.

questions.explanation: A batch request **can't pause for your code**. If Claude calls a client tool you implemented, such as `lookup_vendor`, that request simply ends with a `tool_use` block: nothing runs the tool and continues the conversation inside the same request (the exam guide's "no multi-turn tool calling within a single request"). Batches do accept tool definitions, Anthropic-run server tools and multi-turn message histories you supply, but your own tool still needs a round trip. Here the lookup needs nothing from Claude: the tax ID is already parsed at ingestion, so it is a deterministic database call. Do it in code **before** submitting and include the canonical record in the request. Each document then becomes a single-turn request that fits batch processing.

whyWrong.A: Batch requests may include tool definitions, but nothing executes a client tool and returns its result inside that request. The request would end at the tool_use block with the lookup unanswered.
whyWrong.B: This is false. The batch docs list tool use (including server tools) and multi-turn conversations as supported. The real limit is that your own client tool can't be executed and its result returned in the middle of a request.
whyWrong.D: It works, but each round can take up to 24 hours and every round needs its own correlation logic. Doing the lookup up front is simpler and faster.

questions.mindset: To batch a tool-using workload, move the tool calls out of the request: resolve deterministic lookups in code first so each request finishes in one turn.

questions.stem: You are about to run a one-time backfill of 250,000 scanned support transcripts through a newly written classification prompt using the Message Batches API. The prompt has only been tried on a handful of hand-picked transcripts. What should you do BEFORE submitting the full backfill to keep total cost and rework lowest?

options.text: Run the prompt on a representative sample that includes messy and edge-case transcripts, fix the failures, then batch the full set.
Submit the full backfill at once, then resubmit whatever comes back wrong by custom_id, since the batch discount keeps reruns cheap.
Add a step to the prompt that asks Claude to double-check its own classification before returning it, so the first pass is more accurate.
Switch the backfill to the most capable model available, so prompt weaknesses get compensated for without spending time iterating.

questions.explanation: **Refine the prompt on a sample set before batch-processing large volumes.** Testing on a representative sample, including the edge cases, finds systematic prompt problems cheaply and raises the first-pass success rate. That avoids paying to process, and then reprocess, 250,000 transcripts. The batch docs also recommend checking request shape against the Messages API first, because batch validation errors appear only after the whole batch ends.

whyWrong.B: A 50% discount on a run that has to be repeated is still waste. A systematic prompt flaw could mean resubmitting a large share of 250,000 requests.
whyWrong.C: Self-checking adds tokens to every request and doesn't reliably catch errors that come from a flawed prompt design.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model raises the cost of every request and still leaves untested prompt problems that a cheap sample run would have shown.

questions.mindset: Before a large batch, iterate on a representative sample; scale the prompt only after it is right.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. A coordinator agent built with the Claude Agent SDK delegates to subagents that search the web, analyze documents, synthesize findings and write cited reports.
questions.stem: The research team keeps a 1,500-question regression suite for the report-synthesis prompt. It runs every night against the current prompt, and results are reviewed the next morning. It currently fires 1,500 synchronous calls in parallel, costs a lot and often hits rate limits. Which change BEST cuts the cost while keeping the eval meaningful?

options.text: Run the nightly suite on the smallest, cheapest model, since regression testing only needs to show whether outputs changed between runs.
Submit the nightly suite as a Message Batch, giving each request a custom_id tied to its question ID for grading the next morning.
Cut the suite to the 50 questions that failed most often in the past, so each nightly run uses a fraction of the current token volume.
Keep the synchronous calls but add retry with exponential backoff so that the parallel requests stop failing on rate limits overnight.

questions.explanation: A nightly eval reviewed the next morning is **latency-tolerant and non-blocking**, which fits the Message Batches API well. Large-scale evaluation is one of its listed use cases. The batch gives a 50% discount, higher throughput without managing parallel calls yourself, and reliable grading through `custom_id`. The eval still tests the same prompt on the same model.

whyWrong.A: Changing the model changes what you measure. The eval would no longer test the production setup.
whyWrong.C: Shrinking the suite reduces coverage and misses regressions in cases that used to pass. That weakens the eval.
whyWrong.D: Backoff fixes the rate-limit failures but leaves the full price in place, and price is the main complaint.

questions.mindset: Overnight evals with results reviewed later are a textbook batch workload: same model, same suite, half the price.

questions.scenario: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code runs in your CI/CD pipeline to review pull requests, generate tests and post feedback. Feedback must be actionable, and false positives erode developer trust.
questions.stem: The pre-merge review job is the largest Claude cost in your CI pipeline. Each run sends a long, unchanging set of review guidelines plus the entire repository's key files, then the PR diff. Developers wait on this check before they can merge. Leadership wants the lowest cost without delaying merges. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move the pre-merge review to the Message Batches API and poll every few minutes until the result is ready, to get the 50% discount.
Put the unchanging review guidelines at the start of the prompt and enable prompt caching so that later runs reuse that prefix.
Send only the diff and the files it touches or depends on, instead of the whole set of key repository files on every run.
Place the PR diff first and the review guidelines after it, then mark the guidelines with cache_control so they are reused across runs.
Switch every review to the smallest model regardless of review quality, since the check runs on each PR and saves the most there.

questions.explanation: The check is **blocking**, so it has to stay synchronous. You lower its cost on that synchronous path. **Prompt caching** a stable prefix (the unchanging guidelines) cuts the cost and time of reprocessing repeated input, and **trimming the context** to the diff and related files reduces input tokens on every run. Neither change delays merges.

whyWrong.A: Batch processing can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. Polling doesn't make it faster, and merges could stall.
whyWrong.D: Caching is prefix-based. Everything up to the cache breakpoint must be identical for a hit, so putting the ever-changing diff before the guidelines means the prefix differs on every run and nothing is reused. Static content goes first.
whyWrong.E: Choosing a model 'regardless of quality' sacrifices how well the review catches problems. Model choice should match the task, not only the price.

questions.mindset: Hidden qualifier: 'without delaying merges' rules out batch, so reduce cost within the synchronous path: cache a static prefix placed first, and send less context.
